title: Judicial Renaissance -- Ch. 13: The Power of Example
keywords: The Task of Building a Better Nation
Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr.
Code of Conduct and Ethical Standard for Public Officials and Employees
human dignity as the first article of faith
primary_topics: Chapter 13 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- CJP's remarks at the launch of Jovito R. Salonga's book 'The Task of Building a Better Nation,' arguing that a free and prosperous country depends above all on the fitness of its leaders and on government by example.

The comparison between the Philippines and the post-Soviet emerging democracies: both moved from authoritarian rule and controlled economies to democracy and free enterprise, and both now face the problem of how to advance the economy within the new democratic setting.

Salonga's diagnosis of the three interrelated Philippine maladies -- massive poverty, rampant corruption and uncontrolled criminality -- and his prescription of an open, pluralistic and free society that safeguards liberty and nurtures prosperity, addressed above all to the youth.
Salonga's own life as the proof of his thesis: dissolving his law firm on appointment to the PCGG, living austerely in public office, and authoring the ethics, anti-plunder and anti-coup laws.
sub_topics: CJP recounts attending the 13th International Judicial Conference in Kiev with Chief Justice Davide, alongside chief justices from former Soviet republics and former Soviet allies.

The conference theme was the independence of courts and their role in safeguarding elections -- a tribute to the Ukrainian Supreme Court, which annulled the fraud-ridden presidential election and paved the way for the December 26, 2004 balloting that brought Viktor Yushchenko to power.
What impressed him more than the sessions were the 'corridor conversations' with senior justices from those countries about life after the collapse of the USSR.

Under authoritarian rule everyone had a job but nobody worked; free enterprise, privatization, deregulation and globalization brought efficiency but also layoffs, the withdrawal of subsidies, unemployment and inflation.

He argues the Philippines is comparable to those states: twenty years of Marcos's autocratic rule ended only in 1986, and the yellow People Power revolution inspired the velvet revolutions of 1989 and Ukraine's orange revolution of 2004.

Salonga's book identifies three interrelated main problems -- massive poverty, rampant corruption and uncontrolled criminality -- traced to the concentration of wealth and power in an elite and a double standard of justice.

The book is addressed to the youth, with Salonga's roll of young leaders: Rizal at 26, Bonifacio at 26, Aguinaldo at 29, Mabini at 34, Osmeña, Quezon, Laurel and Roxas in their late twenties and early thirties, and Christ and his disciples in their early thirties.
CJP adds Salonga himself to that roll -- the youngest law dean in the Philippines in his thirties, whose first privileged speech, 'A Plea for Sobriety,' enthralled the country.

Salonga treats the judiciary as an essential ingredient of good government, upholding not only civil and political rights but economic rights; his late law partner and best friend Pedro L. Yap became Chief Justice in 1988.

CJP endorses that discourse from his own conviction that the rule of law is a prerequisite for good governance and development, and that those with less in life should have a better chance at competing with those who have more in law.
Salonga's book defends Chief Justice Davide as innocent of the impeachment charges, which he says were pursued in ruthless, cold-blooded haste to influence pending cases.
Salonga's solution rests on human dignity as the 'first article of faith' -- politically, the sacred worth of every human being; economically, the right of every Filipino to a decent life.
CJP notes a former Singaporean prime minister's complaint that Filipinos have 'too much freedom,' and the resulting timidity of officials who fear media criticism and litigation.

He observes that political rights were restored in 1986 but free enterprise has not worked: huge external debt, gargantuan deficits, escalating inflation and a battered currency, with a lucky few growing richer.
What distinguishes Salonga from politicians who mouth the same slogans is his insistence, after Confucius, that government must be government by example and depends on the fitness of its leaders.
As first PCGG chairman in 1986 Salonga not only divested his conflicting interests as the law required, he dissolved his prestigious law firm, which no law required.

His austerity in office -- a modest rented house, a mid-size locally assembled car, white cotton barongs, no smoking, drinking or gambling -- won him the Mahatma Gandhi Freedom Award from the College of William and Mary.
In the Senate he carried the same austerity and steered the passage of the ethics Code of Conduct, the Anti-Plunder Act and the Anti-Coup d'Etat Law, all of which he authored.
Though counsel to some of the country's biggest companies and three times Number One Senator, he forsook money-making opportunities and dropped supporters whose practices clashed with his work ethic.
At 85 and in retirement he remains healthy, intellectually vibrant and outraged by public excesses, still living by the power of his example.

CJP closes with the 1971 Plaza Miranda grenade attack that left Salonga briefly 'clinically dead,' and answers Salonga's question about God's purpose in sparing him: to be a beacon in a darkened country.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 13 of 'Judicial Renaissance' collects Justice Panganiban's remarks at the launch of Jovito R. Salonga's book 'The Task of Building a Better Nation.' He opened with the 13th International Judicial Conference in Kiev, which he attended with Chief Justice Davide alongside chief justices from former Soviet republics and allies, and whose theme -- judicial independence and the courts' role in safeguarding elections -- honored the Ukrainian Supreme Court for annulling a fraud-ridden presidential election and clearing the way for the balloting that brought Viktor Yushchenko to power. What struck him more than the sessions were the 'corridor conversations' about life after the USSR's collapse: under authoritarian rule everyone had a job but nobody was working, while privatization, deregulation and globalization brought efficiency together with unemployment and inflation. He argued that the Philippines, freed from twenty years of Marcos rule only in 1986, was comparable to those states, and that the yellow People Power revolution had presaged the velvet revolutions of 1989 and Ukraine's orange revolution. Turning to Salonga's book, he set out its diagnosis of three interrelated maladies -- massive poverty, rampant corruption and uncontrolled criminality -- traced to the concentration of wealth in an elite and to a double standard of justice, and its address to the youth, supported by a roll of young leaders from Rizal and Bonifacio to Quezon and Roxas, to which he added the young Salonga himself. He endorsed the book's treatment of the judiciary as guarantor of civil, political and economic rights, repeated his own conviction that those with less in life should have a better chance at competing with those who have more in law, and noted Salonga's defence of Chief Justice Davide against impeachment charges pursued in ruthless, cold-blooded haste. Salonga's prescription -- an open, pluralistic and free society resting on human dignity as the first article of faith -- is distinguished from politicians' copycat incantations, he said, by Salonga's insistence after Confucius that government must be government by example: dissolving his law firm on appointment to the PCGG, living austerely in a rented house with a small car and cotton barongs, authoring the ethics, anti-plunder and anti-coup laws, and forsaking wealth for service. He closed with the 1971 Plaza Miranda grenade attack that left Salonga briefly clinically dead, answering the honoree's question about God's purpose in sparing him: to be a beacon in a darkened country.
